chapter_theme: Three songs at Pattaliyur (பட்டாலியூர்) in Kongu: the killing eyes of women and the wish to serve before grey hair comes, a rejection of sectarian argument and even of mantra and yantra lore in favour of the highest state, and a long praise of the shrine's fierce goddess.
structure_note: 939 catalogues women's eyes and praises the goddess Bhairavi; 940 asks for service while youth lasts; 941 turns away from the debates of the six faiths.

939.reading: The poet lists what women's eyes do: they strike the earrings, outrage the lotus, put even Yama's men to flight, cut a man as nectar mixed with poison, practise Kama's arts, melt even sages with cunning glances, speak of a desire to steal wealth and quarrel as if the age were ending; he asks whether a day will come when, instead of falling into the pit of infatuation these eyes give, he lives in the shade of Murugan's feet. The praise calls him the life of Vayalur on the emerald-feathered peacock, and then names the goddess at length, the trident-bearing Malini, the refuge, the lion-rider, the Mohini of those who drink liquor, the Kali whose goblins dance at the drum-beaten cremation ground, the Bhairavi of Pattaliyur.
939.nuance: Every line of the first half ends in a verb of the eyes (மோதுவ, சீறுவ, மீளுவ, நாடுவ), so the whole plea is built as one sentence about them, ending in உயிர்வதை நயனம், eyes that torture life. The praise gives more space to the goddess, a cremation-ground Kali and Bhairavi worshipped with liquor (மதுபானம் பருகினர்), than to Murugan; several of her epithets (சாதகி, யாமளி, வித்தாரி) are obscure.

940.reading: The poet describes women whose breasts, rubbed with musk, agil, sandal and camphor and hung with pearl chains, strain against the bodice, and asks that he not drink their lips as honey and melt like wax in a smith's furnace; while youth is strong, before his hair turns white as a crane, he asks to be shown the way of humble service at Murugan's feet. The praise names Vayalur within golden walls, recalls the story of Paravai in the pain of separation and the true messenger who hurried to her, calls Murugan the supreme guru, and ends at Pattali where peacocks dance in groves of green palmyra.
940.nuance: கொக்காக நரைகள் வரும் முன்: the plea sets a deadline, service while the body is still young. குற்றேவல் அடிமை is humble service, the book's word for devotion. The lines on பரவை and the மெய்த்தூதர் recall Siva going as messenger to Paravai for Sundarar; how Murugan is tied to that story (as the one who grants it, or as Siva's own form) is not clear.

941.reading: The poet says 'enough, enough' to hearing the clamour of the six faiths arguing their many arts of knowledge, to hearing of the wealth of those who make worship for gain, and even to hearing the mantra, its arrangements, the darshanas and the yantras of the Saiva texts that the consort of Himavan's daughter taught the sages; he asks that, no longer wandering in vain, he be given the highest state. The praise names Murugan the nephew of Rama, who sent Sugriva's army to Lanka, the lord of Vayalur with its areca groves, and the young one at Pattali in Kongu who bowed to the forest girl, likened her breasts, hands and hair to the northern mountain, flowers and cloud, and spoke sweet words of love.
941.nuance: The refusal reaches past the sectarians to the Saiva scriptures themselves: சிவநூலின் மந்த்ரப்ரஸ்தார தரிசன யந்த்ரத்துக் கேள்வி அலமலம். The highest state (பரகதி) is set above hearing even Siva's own mantra lore. The praise ends with Murugan himself humbled in love, bowing to Valli (கும்பிட்டுக் காதல் குனகிய).

links.note: Both take the coming of grey hair as the reason to turn now: the Naladiyar's wise renounce in childhood knowing old age will come, and 940 asks for service at the feet while youth lasts, before the hair whitens like a crane.

Both turn from the uproar of the six faiths and the arts of argument: 941 says 'enough' even to Siva's mantra and yantra lore and asks for the highest state, 951 asks to leave the attachment to argument and know the knowledge that cannot be pointed to.
